Probabilistic lithium-ion battery state-of-health prediction using
convolutional neural networks and Gaussian process regression
Sean Buchanan, Curran Crawford ∗
Institute for Integrated Energy Systems at University of Victoria (IESVic), Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Victoria, 3800 Finnerty
Rd, Victoria, V8P 5C2, BC, Canada
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Integrated gradients
CNN
GPR
Partial charge
Probabilistic state-of-health prediction
A B S T R A C T
As the world accelerates its renewable energy transition, lithium-ion batteries are increasingly being used for
large scale energy storage. Due to the high cost of production and replacement of large lithium-ion battery
packs, accurate estimation of battery state-of-health (SOH) has become important. Accurate estimation is
especially important for microgrid and transportation industries where operational batteries will be charged
intermittently and incompletely. Incomplete charging scenarios provide models with inconsistent inputs, hence,
cause inconsistent output accuracies, which are important to quantify in the context of dispatch controllers and
predictive maintenance. In this paper, we present a model that provides a probabilistic prediction of battery
SOH from periodic charging events as would be encountered in real world operations. The proposed model
combines the feature recognition and many-to-one mapping abilities of the classic convolutional neural network
(CNN) with the probabilistic characteristics of Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) models. The combined CNN-
GPR model predicts battery SOH to less than 1% mean absolute error using random partial charge segments
as input and displays its confidence in the prediction using the variance from the GPR. Additionally, the CNN-
GPR is able to predict battery SOH irrespective of battery usage history; this is demonstrated by validation on
dynamic data sets where the model achieves a mean absolute error of less than 1% despite only being trained
on standardized degradation cycles.
1. Introduction
Lithium-ion batteries degrade based on complex interactions be-
tween external and internal conditions, namely temperature, current,
voltage, and battery usage, where the battery usage can differ widely
depending on the application mean state-of-charge (SOC), depth-of-
discharge (DOD), and C-rates. Since most realistic usage conditions
can only be approximated, it is of great interest to accurately estimate
battery health independently of its usage.
Unfortunately, many of the methods used to estimate battery health
are dependent on battery usage. In [ 1] Tian argues that all methods,
both dependent on and independent of battery usage, can be classified
into four main categories: model-based methods, hybrid methods, other
methods, and data-driven methods. Some examples of model based
methods are presented in [ 2,3], and [ 4] which leverage models built
from a physical foundation such as electrochemical, equivalent circuit,
or semi-empirical derivation methods. The model-based methods pro-
vide sufficient accuracy; unfortunately, they rarely provide methods for
adapting to the change in their parameters, as batteries degrade and
do not adapt well to varying battery usage. To improve the accuracy

of model-based methods, some have combined them with data-driven
methods in an attempt to harness the benefits of both methods. In [ 5]
an empirical model is derived from first principles and combined with
a back-propagation neural network (BPNN) to predict and compensate
for the error of the empirical model. The model achieves a mean
absolute error (MAE) of approximately 2%, however, it still relies on
full charge cycles for data processing and is not validated on a dynamic
data set. Nevertheless, hybrid methods show promising abilities to
achieve more accurate results than model-based methods, while being
more robust to unknown inputs than purely data-driven methods.
Unfortunately, the model-based portion of the model may still require
specialized tests to fit model parameters which can be time consuming
and difficult to perform accurately. Another offshoot of hybrid methods
classified as ‘‘other’’ by Tian, contains the popular incremental capacity
analysis (ICA) method, which attempts to extract degradation features
from a battery’s capacity-voltage curve by calculating the derivative of
capacity with respect to voltage. In [ 6], battery capacity is predicted
to within 1% using ICA and support vector regression (SVR) on partial
charging data. The SVR in [6] is used to reduce the method’s sensitivity

to the range of partial charging data used, however, it is still more
susceptible to noise than other methods, undermining its performance
in practical applications.
The last category explored is data-driven methods. Data-driven
methods have become increasingly popular because they provide the
opportunity to accurately model the relationship between observed
measurements and battery SOH without the need to fully model or
understand the internal workings of the battery. This is especially useful
for the modeling of lithium-ion batteries because of their complex
side reactions and non-linear degradation behavior [7]. Consequently,
there are many studies demonstrating the success of different machine
learning algorithms such as support vector machines [8], temporal con-
volutional networks [9], feed-forward neural networks and long-short-
term-memory (LSTM) [10], Gaussian process regression (GPR) [11,12],
and convolutional neural networks (CNN) [10,13,14]. Although all of
the mentioned methods are intriguing in their own right, the ability of
the CNN to reduce multiple contemporaneous features down to a single
output makes it well suited for the case where multiple time-series
inputs (i.e. 𝑉 , 𝐼) are being mapped to a single SOH value. This CNN
characteristic is apparent in [13] where a CNN is used to predict battery
SOH using partial voltage, current, and temperature charge profiles as
input. The model achieved a MAE of less than 2% with noise added to
the data to demonstrate model robustness. However, the practicality of
this model is undermined by the need to train a new model for every
SOC range that is used as input. In [14] a CNN is used with partial
voltage and current charge data to predict battery capacity. The partial
charges in this case all still contain the constant voltage portion of
the charge data, requiring users to fully charge their device to 100%
SOC to use the model. Additionally, the method in [14] requires new
models to be trained for every charge segment that is used as data.
In [15,16] a CNN is combined with the LSTM architecture to better
predict battery remaining-useful-life. In [17] a CNN is combined with
a gated recurrent unit network to improve the estimation of battery
SOH. The combination of the CNN with network architectures that have
memory ability improves the prediction accuracy and reduces training
time [16]; however, the methods in [15,16], and [17] fail to represent
the difference in estimation accuracy when using partial, instead of full,
charges as model input.
In general, papers using the presented machine learning methods
are absent of a metric that illustrates how confident the model is in its
prediction. Probabilistic prediction is demonstrated in [12] where GPR
is used to predict battery capacity purely from partial voltage charge
data. The voltage data is segmented based on a lower and upper voltage
bound so that they are independent of SOC. Unfortunately, this means
that the model is only trained for a specific voltage segment. In [11]
a sparse GPR method is used to predict battery SOH from capacity
change. The capacity change is calculated from partial segments of
the voltage vs capacity curve. The draw back to this approach is that
the partial segments do not account for unique charging times and the
sparse GPR requires a significant number of inducing points (500) to
produce a sufficiently accurate prediction.
The stated drawbacks of the discussed papers are addressed in this
paper by aiming to provide a model that is easily implemented, practi-
cal, and provides probabilistic predictions. To ease implementation, a
CNN is leveraged to extract features from unprocessed charging data.
To improve practicality, the CNN is trained on partial charge segments
that have a random beginning SOC between 15 and 85 percent and a
random charge length between 30 and 115 min at 0.3C; partitioning the
data in such a way ensures that the model does not require a consistent
portion of charge data to predict the battery SOH, as would be the case
for real operational usage cases. Finally, sparse GPR is used to operate
on the CNN predictions to capture the variation in CNN prediction
accuracy from the inconsistent input characterization charge cycles and
produce a meaningful, error bound, result for the user. By operating
on the CNN output, rather than directly on the input, the number of
required inducing points in the sparse GPR is greatly reduced from
hundreds down to just 20, improving computational efficiency, and
therefore practicality of the model while maintaining the benefits of the
GPR through its probabilistic predictions. Such a model will be useful
in electric fleet management where vehicle charging is inconsistent,
resulting in partial charges at different ranges of SOC. Because different
ranges of SOC will provide different prediction accuracies, providing
error bounds on the prediction will enable fleet managers to make more
confident decisions by reliably identifying ESSs that are out of normal
ranges within the fleet. Additionally, providing error metrics on the
SOH prediction will allow battery management systems to operate more
accurately under partial charging conditions as present in microgrid
applications requiring real time dispatch controllers.
The remainder of this paper describes the test setup and data
collection in Section 2, the Data-Driven CNN in Section 3, the CNN-
only model tuning in Section 4, the models relationship to the data
through integrated gradients in Section 5, the method for sampling
random partial charge cycles in Section 6, and finally a discussion of
the combined CNN-GPR in Section 7 followed by conclusions.
2. Data collection and experiment design
The data used for training and validation in this paper is from ex-
periments performed at the Pacific Regional Institute of Marine Energy
Discovery (PRIMED) Battery Lab. The batteries used are the Mollicel
P42A [18] with parameters shown in Table 1.
The battery cycling was performed by an Arbin LBT 60 A, 16
channel, cell testing cabinet and the ambient temperature control was
performed by a Thermotron S-8-8200 environmental chamber. The
cycling of the 16 batteries, 1 per channel, followed the same general
schedule of 14 days of degradation cycling intersected with a character-
ization cycle. Twelve of the sixteen channels were cycled with constant
current charge/discharge cycles with different𝐷𝑂𝐷𝑖 and 𝐶𝑖. Two of the
remaining channels were cycled with a dynamic degradation cycle that
was designed to approximate the charge discharge pattern of an ESS
connected to a solar array. The final two channels were calendar ageing
cycles, hence, maintained a rest state for the degradation cycle. The
characterization, static degradation, and dynamic degradation cycles
are described in the following subsections.

3. Data-driven CNN model
The motivation for the CNN model was to map charge profiles to
SOH values to see if a model could be developed that is independent
of the degradation discharge/charge profile (a.k.a battery history).
The CNN architecture was chosen because of its ability to map the
multidimensional time-series data to a single SOH value and its proven
success in similar applications in [ 13,14].
The data used to train the CNN was the CC and CV charge time-
series from the characterization cycles, which are aligned in time
such that at a SOC of zero (minimum voltage), time equals zero.
The inclusion of battery temperature in the dataset was considered;
however, preliminary tests with the model showed no improvement
with temperature as an input. Consequently, the model operates under
the reasonable assumption that the ambient temperature is controlled

First, the characterization cycle contains the most precise measurement

independence can be easily tested. To increase ease of implementation
and practicality of the model the data processing was kept to a mini-

sampled from a data point every 5 s to a data point every 35 s, corre-

SOC per step at the characterization cycle charge rate of 1/3C. Down-
sampling in this way has no impact on the data quality because the
system dynamics are slow enough that a sample every 35 s is sufficient.
Next, the charge profiles were resized to fulfill the CNN constraint of
consistently sized input. To ensure the consistent length of the charge
cycles the non-uniform charge times were simply extended at their final
values until they were the same length as the longest charge time.
The data set modification only extends the constant voltage and zero
current portions of the charge profiles which has a negligible effect on
model accuracy because it is the least informative data. The extension
of the data is illustrated in Fig. 3 .
Once the charge profiles are processed they are concatenated into
an input array of dimensions (m 𝑥 n 𝑥 c) where m is the number of
characterization charge cycles, n is the length of the time series (same
for every charge cycle), and c is the number of channels (which is 2
because there are voltage and current channels). Since one combined
voltage and current charge profile is being mapped to one SOH value, it
follows that the output is a (m𝑥 1) array of SOH values. During training
and validation 𝑚 > 1; however, when using the trained model 𝑚 = 1 as
shown in Fig. 4.
4. CNN-only model tuning
This section describes the process of tuning the CNN to obtain an
optimal model. Because of the proliferation of machine learning plat-
forms such as Tensorflow and PyTorch the implementation of common
machine learning models has become relatively simple. Additionally,
it is the authors’ belief that a summary of the mathematics behind
CNN’s and a discussion of how they work is unnecessary as there are
many great resources that will provide better material, including [ 19].
Consequently, only a brief overview of CNN concepts will be presented
and the rest of this section will focus on the impact of various hyper-
parameters and the insight gained from analyzing the results in the
specific application of lithium-ion battery SOH prediction.
In general, a CNN can be viewed as a feature extractor or detec-
tor. In the simplest sense, a CNN layer achieves feature detection by
convolving a kernel over the input, and operating on the kernel output
with an activation function plus a bias. In Fig. 4 the first convolution
layer has 5 randomly initialized kernels with a length of 5 that all
independently sweep over the input and produce their own output,
resulting in 5 filters. Following the first layer is a max pooling layer
where the kernel of length 2 simply selects the maximum value within
the kernel window, reducing the size of the filters by a factor of the
kernel length. The rest of the model continues on similarly until it
reaches the output.
Before the hyperparameters of the tuned model in Fig. 4 were
determined an educated guess about the initial model architecture was
required. The initial guess was to use two 1D convolution layers with
max pooling between layers, a flattening layer following the CNN, and
a final fully connected layer to a single SOH prediction as depicted
in Fig. 4 . The two CNN layer parameters were 16 and 32 filters, a
sweep of 1, a kernel size of 5, and a ReLu activation function. The
final fully connected layer was initialized to 64 neurons with ReLu
activation functions. Next, the model was trained for 500 epochs on all
of the characterization charge cycles from channels 1, 2, 4, 9, 11, 12,
13, 14, and 15 and validated on the cycles from channels 3, 10, and
16; an approximately 70/30 split. This results in 153 distinct charge
profiles at varying SOH’s for training. The relatively small training set
provides an opportunity to test how the model handles smaller datasets
characteristic of battery testing campaigns due to the long time needed
for degradation. Additionally, the model is evaluated on the dynamic
charge data of channels 6 and 7 to evaluate the models performance
on dynamic data. The results are shown in Figs. 5 and 6 and the MAE
is presented in row one of Table 3 .
The prediction error is remarkably low for a first guess. Regardless,
the model must still be analyzed so that areas of improvement can be
identified. First, we define improvement as a reduction in prediction
error or a reduction in model size while maintaining or reducing the
current prediction error.
There are two likely avenues for reducing the error. First, a larger
model with regularization could be built. Second, smaller models can
be tested to see if the current model is over-parameterized. Due to the
initial models high performance, it is unlikely that the prediction error
will reduce significantly with a larger model. Additionally, it is likely
that a reduction in model size (number of parameters) would be more
useful in most practical situations; therefore, multiple smaller models
are trained and evaluated to study the effect of hyperparameters on the
model fit.
Because the initial model provided remarkable results, the general
architecture is retained and only the parameters within the layers are
varied. Consequently, the number of filters in the first and second

5. Integrated gradients results analysis
Although the CNN model achieves impressive results it is imprac-
tical to assume that a full charge, from 0 to 100% SOC as defined by
cut-off voltages, will be regularly encountered during a battery’s life-
time. In real use cases, batteries are discharged and charged arbitrarily

over their SOC ranges. Consequently, an investigation of the models
interpretation of the data was performed to understand which portions
of the charge cycle are most informative. To interpret the relationship
between data and model, the method of integrated gradients (IG) was
used [ 20–22]. IG is commonly used when performing classification,
especially in the case of classifying images, however, it is rarely used in
regression circumstances. The method calculates the change in model
prediction accuracy with respect to a data points distance from a
baseline (gradient). In terms of images, this would mean the impact
a pixel has on image recognition as it transitions from black (the
baseline) to its final color and brightness. In terms of charge segments,
the choice of baseline is much more difficult. Multiple baselines were
experimented with until the baseline of a new battery charge segment
was chosen. The baseline analysis can be seen in the accompanying
GitHub repository1 where the baseline is selected to be the charge cycle
of a new battery.

data point. Finally, the IG attributions are calculated by integrating the
gradients using the Reimann trapezoidal integral approximation. The
resulting attributions represent the importance of each data point in
each charge profile (voltage or current) and are plotted as a heatmap
along the charge profile curves as shown in Figs. 10 and 11 , where 1
in the color bar signifies most important and 0 signifies least important
points.
What do the results in Figs. 10 and 11 say about the model and how
it interprets the data? The most obvious observation is that the model
finds the region of minimum voltage to approximately 3.7 V relatively
uninformative for both voltage and current data. Next, there is a region
of mild importance from 3.8 V to 4.0 V with increasing importance
after 4.0 V until maximum voltage is reached. Additionally, there
appears to be a vertical correlation in attribution intensity suggesting
a time dependence. The time dependence indicates that the relative
orientation of the charge cycles in time is important, confirming our
decision at the beginning of the paper to align the charge profiles in
time. Finally, there is a noticeable increase in attribution magnitude
around areas of curvature suggesting that the model is gaining more
insight from the nonlinear portions of the data.
It is important that the insight gained from the IG method is
leveraged to improve the practicality of the model by either reducing
the amount of data needed for training and predicting, improving

the predictive performance of the model, or making the model more

less data because IG shows us that the most informative data is near the
end of the charge cycle where the probability of it being encountered
consistently is low. Improving the performance of the model is not
practical either because it already has such a low prediction error.
Consequently, the improvements of the model must stem from areas
in flexibility, generalization, and robustness. To improve these factors,
the model should ideally work on any charge segment, not just the full
charge data or some specific subset of a full charge.
From the IG results it is evident that training a model on random
charge segments would result in varied prediction accuracy depending
on the length and location of the data in the charge cycle. The intro-
duced randomness in the input and variance in the output suggests
that a probabilistic model can be built that provides a mean and
variance for the predictions based on which portion of charge is used.
A natural extension of this realization is to create a combined CNN and
GPR model that provides probabilistic predictions. The probabilistic
predictions will inform users of the model accuracy given what portion
of charge it receives as input with the expectation that opportunistic CV
portions of the charging profile will have lower uncertainty compared
to CC and lower voltage segments. The creation and results of the new
CNN-GPR model are described in Section 7 .
6. Partial charge cycle data processing
To simulate the partial charge cycles that a battery is likely to
encounter in its lifetime, additional data was created by randomly
sampling from the existing characterization charge cycles. The random
cycle sampling consists of three processes: removing bias, sampling
from the full charge cycles, and aligning the partial charges in time.
All three processes are described in the following subsections.

6.1. Removing bias
The bias in the dataset stems from the fact that the batteries
have different levels of final degradation after the complete testing
campaign, given the range of C-rates and DOD’s used across the set
of batteries. Consequently, there are many more data points in the
mid SOH region than the low SOH region. This bias has a negligible
impact when training with full charge cycles because there are rela-
tively few training charge profiles (approximately 150). However, when
the data is augmented with duplicated charge cycles the number of
charge profiles increases, hence, the bias increases. To explain the data
augmenting process we define the dataset as a set of voltage and current
charge profile input array’s, 𝐼𝑖,𝑗, and output SOH’s, 𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝑖,𝑗, where 𝑖 is
the bin number and 𝑗 is the sample number. The SOH’s are then sorted
into 𝑁 evenly spaced bins, where 𝑁 = 5 for this paper, and each bin
has a number 𝑛𝑖 of 𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝑖,𝑗’s in it . To remove the bias introduced by the
inequality between the 𝑛𝑖’s, the 𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝑖,𝑗 and their corresponding input
arrays 𝐼𝑖,𝑗 in each under represented bin are duplicated until all 𝑛𝑖’s are
equal. A visual representation of the bins is shown in Fig. 12 .
6.2. Random sampling
The random sampling is parameterized by two variables, one global
constraint, and one conditional constraint. Beginning SOC ( 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏) and
segment length in units of time ( 𝑆𝐿) are the variables of the sampling
process. The global constraint constrains the segment length in time
to span a change in SOC of at least 10%. The conditional constraint
ensures that the beginning voltage of a charge cycle is less than 4.10 V;
this constraint is conditional because it is only applied to validation
data. The conditional constraint reduces the maximum prediction error
by ensuring that the charge segment contains some non-constant volt-
age data. This approach is practically relevant as it is unlikely that the
voltage will not drop below its maximum before a system is recharged.
To perform the random cycle sampling, an augmented dataset as
described in Section 6.1 is produced. Then, for every charge profile
𝐼𝑖,𝑗 in the dataset, a new beginning SOC ( 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏) and length of charge
(𝑆𝐿) is selected from discrete uniform distributions between 15 and
85 percent, and 30 and 115 min, respectively. The portion of the
original full charge segment starting at 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏 and continuing for a
length of time 𝑆𝐿 is then extracted to make a new partial input charge
segment 𝐼𝑝𝑐 𝑖,𝑗. The new partial charge segment and its corresponding
SOH label 𝑆𝑂𝐻𝑝𝑐 𝑖,𝑗 are then added to the partial charge dataset. This
process is repeated multiple times for each full charge profile,𝐼𝑖,𝑗, in the
augmented dataset until a sufficient number of partial charge segments
have been added to the partial charge dataset.

6.3. Aligning partial charge segments
The IG analysis in Section 5 showed that the model relies on the
charge segments being consistently aligned in time. Hence, the partial
charge segments also need to be aligned in time to maintain the
models prediction accuracy. In Section 3 it is stated that the full charge
segments are aligned in time such that 𝑡 = 0 at 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏 = 0 for all charge
cycles; however, now that 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏 ≠ 0, 𝑡 must be shifted from zero such
that the partial charge cycle maintains its position in time relative to
the charge cycle of a new battery. Since 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏 always occurs within
the CC portion of the charge cycle it will always lie on the linear,
highlighted, portion of Fig. 13 where all charge profiles overlap with
the new battery charge cycle regardless of their SOH since the charging
rate is the same in all cases.
If we define time as a function of new battery SOC ( 𝑡(𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑛𝑒𝑤))
then to ensure the same position for the partial charge cycles relative
to a new charge cycle, the partial charge cycles are shifted such that
𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑛𝑒𝑤 = 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏, giving 𝑡 = 𝑡(𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏) for all partial charges. Once
the partial charge is shifted, its value at the beginning and end of the
segment are appended until it spans the same length of time as a full
charge of a new battery. Fig. 14 illustrates the alignment in time from
𝑡 = 0 to 𝑡(𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑏) of a partial charge cycle, and Fig. 15 demonstrates
how the appended partial charge cycle remains aligned with the full
charge it came from, despite being aligned with 𝑆𝑂𝐶 𝑛𝑒𝑤 from the full
charge cycle.
This method of alignment relies on two assumptions; first, that there
is a reliable model estimating SOC and second, that there is a full charge
cycle, from 0 to 100% SOC, when the battery is new. Both assumptions
are reasonable given the advanced battery management systems in use
today and the fact that new batteries undergo a full charge at beginning
of life.

7. CNN-GPR model
As with the standalone CNN model, explaining the mathematical
nuances of the CNN and GPR model formulations are left to machine-
learning Refs. [19,23]. The GPR will only be summarized and then the
model construction, application, and results will be presented in this
section.
7.1. GPR overview
In general, when trying to map an input–output relationship using
data there are infinite possible functions that can be selected. Gaussian
process regression uses Bayesian inference with a kernel function as a
prior to find a distribution of functions that fit the data with a mean
function that has the highest probability of describing the data.
Mathematically, if the CNN output is the estimated SOH, ̂𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝐶𝑁𝑁 ,
then
̂𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝐶𝑁𝑁 −𝐺𝑃 𝑅 = 𝑓 (̂𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝐶𝑁𝑁 ) (2)
where 𝑓 () is the GPR function and ̂𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝐶𝑁𝑁 −𝐺𝑃 𝑅 is a Gaussian distri-
bution calculated using ̂𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝐶𝑁𝑁 and a kernel [24].
Because the Gaussian process is probabilistic it also provides an
estimate of the models confidence in its prediction. In the CNN-GPR,
the Gaussian process regression relies on Sparse Variational Gaussian
Process’ (SVGP) as defined in the gpflux package [ 24]. The use of
the SVGP algorithm reduces the computational burden of traditional
Gaussian process regression by using inducing points. Additionally,
because the GPR in the CNN-GPR is being trained on the single output
of the CNN instead of the original time-series charge cycles there is
a reduction in training points, further reducing training times when
compared to a stand alone GPR model. The final CNN-GPR model
consists of the CNN model architecture and best parameters presented
in Section 4, combined with a GPR layer as shown in Fig. 16 .
7.2. CNN GPR interaction
Intuitively, one might expect the CNN and GPR to act sequentially
such that the CNN predicts SOH as accurately as possible and then
the GPR fits the CNN estimation to correct for the varying CNN SOH
estimations. Fundamentally, this understanding is the same as if the
CNN and GPR are trained separately. Fig. 17 shows the resulting fit of
a linear kernel GPR trained with the stand alone CNN’s estimated SOH
as input and the measured SOH as output.
Alternatively, if the GPR is added as a final layer to the CNN
such that the CNN and GPR become a single model that is trained as
one, the CNN then becomes a transformer for the GPR. The combined
configuration now causes the CNN to transform its output relative to
the stand alone CNN such that the GPR has the best form of inputs
for its kernel function. Consequently, if there is an expected form for
the CNN output, such as the linear relationship between estimated and
measured SOH’s, then the GPR kernel choice can be used to inform
the CNN of the best way to transform its output to match the expected
output. Effectively, the GPR kernel is no longer just a tool to fit a given
input, but a tool to inform a transformer of the most effective basis
coordinates for accurate GPR estimation. Figs. 17–20 compare the CNN
GPR interaction of a combined CNN-GPR with its independently trained
counterpart for linear and squared exponential kernel selections. The
figures show the models fit to the same training data used throughout
the paper.
Figs. 19 and 20 provide a noticeable shift in model behavior be-
tween independent and combined CNN and GPR, however, it is the
differences between the ̂𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝐶𝑁𝑁 axes in Figs. 17 and 18 that is
most notable. The ̂𝑆𝑂𝐻 𝐶𝑁𝑁 axis in Fig. 18 shows how the CNN
has compressed the output space to increase linearity and reduce the
variance in its output. As expected, the model that provides the lowest
mean average error, mean squared error, and max error is the linear
kernel with the fully connected CNN-GPR architecture. Consequently,
the fully connected CNN-GPR architecture with a linear kernel is the
chosen model and its performance and results will be discussed in the
following section.
7.3. CNN-GPR results and discussion
The CNN-GPR training dataset contains the same 153 full character-

as the original CNN, plus an additional 1,957 partial charge segments
sampled from the full characterization charge segments of the cells
just mentioned, equaling a total of 2,110 training charge cycles. The
validation dataset is split into two subsets; the first contains data from
the CC discharge (static) cycle tests from channels 3, 10 and 16, and
the second contains data from the variable C-rate (dynamic) cycle tests
from channels 6 and 7. The same process was followed as described
in Section 6 to obtain partial charge segments with one difference
compared to the training set. The validation dataset only contains one
partial charge sample ( 𝐼𝑝𝑐 𝑖,𝑗) for every SOH label while the training
dataset contains multiple. The model was trained on an AMD Ryzen 5
5600H 3.3 GHz CPU with 16 GB of RAM for 200 epochs with a duration

charging from 15 to 25% SOC. To reduce the maximum error, the
model is given a reduced operating range. If the operating range limits

More important than the overall error is the similar error resulting
from both the static and dynamic validation datasets, despite the model
only being trained on the static data. This result suggests that the CNN-
GPR accurately predicts battery SOH regardless of how the battery is
cycled for degradation, and is only reliant on periodic and opportunistic
charging cycle segments for effective SOH estimation.
8. Conclusions
This paper investigated the input data/prediction relationship of a
CNN predicting state of health for lithium-ion batteries using the In-
tegrated Gradients method. The Integrated Gradients method revealed
that mid-voltage, high-voltage, and constant voltage charge segments

are all strong predictors of battery state of health. This information
implies that input of randomized charge profile lengths and beginning
state of charge values possess a variance based on which portion of
the charge profile is used. Consequently, the CNN-GPR model was con-
structed to capture this variance and provide a probabilistic prediction
of battery state of health. The probabilistic prediction is especially
useful where partial charges are common and accurate battery lifetime
prognostics are required. Finally, the CNN-GPR performance is tested
on both static and dynamic battery usage data. The CNN-GPR predicts
the battery state of health with less than 0.7% average MAE and 4.5%
maximum absolute error over 100 randomly sampled partial input
charges on dynamic data. Remarkably, the CNN-GPR achieves these
results when it has only been trained on static test data.
To extend the predictive success of the CNN-GPR there are two main
elements that can be improved:
• Validate the model on a separate data set to assess its applicability
to different battery chemistry’s and sizes, potentially utilizing
transfer learning.
• This first version of the CNN-GPR was trained and validated with
uniform C-rate charge profiles and constant ambient temperature.
To improve the practicality of the model, multiple C-rates and
ambient temperatures should be used for training and validation.
With these small changes, this model approach will provide an
opportunity to gather fleet-level insights into SOH based on variable
duty and charge cycles across the fleet and for microgrids with variable
load, genset, and renewable generation profiles.
